items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the progress of a country in improving the economy, living standards, health, education and freedom of its people”.
items.answer: Development
items.markingKey: Development: the progress of a country in improving the economy, living standards, health, education and freedom of its people. [1]

items.stem: Explain why GNI per capita is not a perfect measure of development.
items.answer: It is an average that hides inequality within a country; ignores the informal economy and subsistence farming; ignores quality of life such as health, education and freedom; affected by exchange rates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why life expectancy is higher in HICs than in LICs.
items.answer: Better health care, clean water and sanitation, better diet, vaccinations and safer working conditions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows development indicators for selected countries. Mexico: GNI per capita US$11 000, life expectancy 75 years, HDI 0.78. Brazil: GNI per capita US$9 000, life expectancy 76 years, HDI 0.76. Kenya: GNI per capita US$2 100, life expectancy 63 years, HDI 0.6. Norway: GNI per capita US$95 000, life expectancy 83 years, HDI 0.97. Calculate how many times greater the highest GNI per capita is than the lowest.
items.answer: 45.2 times

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows development indicators for selected countries. Brazil: GNI per capita US$9 000, life expectancy 76 years, HDI 0.76. Japan: GNI per capita US$42 000, life expectancy 84 years, HDI 0.92. China: GNI per capita US$13 000, life expectancy 78 years, HDI 0.79. Norway: GNI per capita US$95 000, life expectancy 83 years, HDI 0.97. Mexico: GNI per capita US$11 000, life expectancy 75 years, HDI 0.78. (a) Rank the countries by HDI from highest to lowest. (b) Suggest why a country may have a high GNI per capita but a lower life expectancy than expected.
items.answer: (a) Norway, Japan, China, Mexico, Brazil (b) Wealth is unequally distributed, little spent on health care, poor diet or lifestyle diseases, conflict or high HIV rates.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows development indicators for selected countries. Bangladesh: GNI per capita US$2 700, life expectancy 73 years, HDI 0.67. Niger: GNI per capita US$600, life expectancy 62 years, HDI 0.39. Kenya: GNI per capita US$2 100, life expectancy 63 years, HDI 0.6. China: GNI per capita US$13 000, life expectancy 78 years, HDI 0.79. India: GNI per capita US$2 400, life expectancy 70 years, HDI 0.64. (a) Calculate how many times greater the highest GNI per capita is than the lowest. (b) Describe the relationship between GNI per capita and life expectancy shown in Table 3.1.
items.answer: (a) 21.7 times (b) Positive: countries with higher GNI per capita generally have higher life expectancy.
items.markingKey: (a) 13 000 ÷ 600 = 21.7 [2] (b) 1 mark relationship; 1 mark data/exception [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows development indicators for selected countries. Niger: GNI per capita US$600, life expectancy 62 years, HDI 0.39. Norway: GNI per capita US$95 000, life expectancy 83 years, HDI 0.97. Japan: GNI per capita US$42 000, life expectancy 84 years, HDI 0.92. India: GNI per capita US$2 400, life expectancy 70 years, HDI 0.64. Kenya: GNI per capita US$2 100, life expectancy 63 years, HDI 0.6. (a) Calculate how many times greater the highest GNI per capita is than the lowest. (b) Suggest one other indicator that could be added to the table, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 158.3 times (b) Literacy rate, infant mortality, access to clean water or doctors per 1000 people – each shows social development not measured by income.
items.markingKey: (a) 95 000 ÷ 600 = 158.3 [2] (b) 1 mark indicator; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows development indicators for selected countries. Norway: GNI per capita US$95 000, life expectancy 83 years, HDI 0.97. Bangladesh: GNI per capita US$2 700, life expectancy 73 years, HDI 0.67. Kenya: GNI per capita US$2 100, life expectancy 63 years, HDI 0.6. China: GNI per capita US$13 000, life expectancy 78 years, HDI 0.79. Japan: GNI per capita US$42 000, life expectancy 84 years, HDI 0.92. (a) Describe the relationship between GNI per capita and life expectancy shown in Table 3.1. (b) Rank the countries by HDI from highest to lowest. (c) Suggest one other indicator that could be added to the table, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Positive: countries with higher GNI per capita generally have higher life expectancy, though Norway is an exception. (b) Norway, Japan, China, Bangladesh, Kenya (c) Literacy rate, infant mortality, access to clean water or doctors per 1000 people – each shows social development not measured by income.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark relationship; 1 mark data/exception [2] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark indicator; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the total value of goods and services produced by a country plus income from abroad, divided by its population”.
items.answer: Gross national income (GNI) per capita
items.markingKey: Gross national income (GNI) per capita: the total value of goods and services produced by a country plus income from abroad, divided by its population. [1]

items.stem: Explain how an increase in literacy can help a country develop.
items.answer: Literate people can get better-paid skilled jobs, understand health information, start businesses and take part in decisions, raising productivity and incomes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: A student tests the hypothesis “Countries with higher GNI per capita have higher life expectancy.” using six countries: UK: US$49 000, 81 years. Mexico: US$11 000, 75 years. Nigeria: US$2 100, 54 years. Norway: US$95 000, 83 years. Kenya: US$2 100, 63 years. India: US$2 400, 70 years. Explain why a sample of six countries limits the conclusion.
items.answer: A small sample may not be representative and the result could be due to chance; more countries from each income group are needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark small/unrepresentative; 1 mark improvement [2]

items.stem: A student tests the hypothesis “Countries with higher GNI per capita have higher life expectancy.” using six countries: China: US$13 000, 78 years. Bangladesh: US$2 700, 73 years. India: US$2 400, 70 years. UK: US$49 000, 81 years. Niger: US$600, 62 years. Japan: US$42 000, 84 years. (a) Rank the countries for GNI per capita and for life expectancy (1 = highest). (b) Calculate Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient using rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n³ − n).
items.answer: (a) China 3/3; Bangladesh 4/4; India 5/5; UK 1/2; Niger 6/6; Japan 2/1 (b) rs = 0.94
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each correct set of ranks (tied values share the mean rank) [2] (b) Σd² = 2; 1 − 6 × 2 ÷ (6³ − 6) = 0.94 [3]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the widening difference in wealth and quality of life between the richest and poorest countries”.
items.answer: Development gap
items.markingKey: Development gap: the widening difference in wealth and quality of life between the richest and poorest countries. [1]

items.stem: Explain why there are inequalities within countries.
items.answer: Core regions attract investment, jobs, services and skilled migrants (cumulative causation), while the periphery is remote, has poor infrastructure and loses young people; physical factors such as climate and relief also matter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark core advantages; 1 mark periphery problems; 1 mark process [3]

items.stem: Explain how colonial history can help explain the development gap.
items.answer: Colonies exported raw materials cheaply and imported manufactured goods; infrastructure was built for export, not development; borders and conflicts left after independence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: For Brazil or another example of regional inequality within a country, briefly describe the pattern of inequality.
items.answer: Brazil: The south-east (São Paulo, Rio) produces over half of Brazil’s GDP; GNI per capita there is about three times that of the north-east (e.g. Maranhão); life expectancy and literacy are lower in the north-east; the Amazon north is sparsely populated with few services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Core and periphery regions named, with income/health/education figures. [4]

items.stem: Study your case study of regional inequality within a country (for example Brazil). Briefly describe the pattern of inequality.
items.answer: Brazil: The south-east (São Paulo, Rio) produces over half of Brazil’s GDP; GNI per capita there is about three times that of the north-east (e.g. Maranhão); life expectancy and literacy are lower in the north-east; the Amazon north is sparsely populated with few services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Core and periphery regions named, with income/health/education figures. [4]

items.stem: With reference to India, or another example of regional inequality within a country you have studied, explain why there are differences in development between regions.
items.answer: Model answer (India): Investment in ports and IT in western and southern states; better education and health spending in Kerala; high population density and reliance on farming in Bihar; poor infrastructure in rural states.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Physical, historical, economic and social causes, cumulative causation. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a wealthy, economically advanced area of a country, often around the capital or main ports”.
items.answer: Core region
items.markingKey: Core region: a wealthy, economically advanced area of a country, often around the capital or main ports. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Inequality only exists between countries, not within them.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Regions within countries differ greatly, e.g. south-east and north-east Brazil.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “jobs that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining”.
items.answer: Primary sector
items.markingKey: Primary sector: jobs that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining. [1]

items.stem: Explain how employment structure changes as a country develops.
items.answer: In LICs most work in the primary sector (farming); industrialisation increases secondary jobs; in HICs mechanisation and deindustrialisation reduce primary and secondary jobs, and most work in tertiary and quaternary services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each stage up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why manufacturing has grown in many NEEs such as China and Vietnam.
items.answer: Cheap, plentiful labour; government incentives and special economic zones; investment by TNCs; improving infrastructure and ports; growing domestic markets.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: In Country Q, 22% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 31% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. Is this country most likely to be an LIC, an NEE or an HIC? Give a reason.
items.answer: NEE: a large secondary sector (31%) as industry grows, with primary falling (22%).
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement; 1 mark use of data [2]

items.stem: In Country R, 1% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 21% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. (a) Calculate the percentage employed in the tertiary sector. (b) Is this country most likely to be an LIC, an NEE or an HIC? Give a reason.
items.answer: (a) 78% (b) HIC: very few in primary (1%) and most in services (78%).
items.markingKey: (a) 100 − 1 − 21 = 78% [1] (b) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark use of data [2]

items.stem: In Country R, 20% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 26% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. (a) Is this country most likely to be an LIC, an NEE or an HIC? Give a reason. (b) Explain how the employment structure may change in the next 30 years.
items.answer: (a) NEE: a large secondary sector (26%) as industry grows, with primary falling (20%). (b) Secondary may peak then fall as wages rise and automation increases; tertiary and quaternary will grow.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark use of data [2] (b) 1 mark change; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Explain why the tertiary sector grows as incomes rise.
items.answer: People can afford more services such as leisure, tourism, health care and education; governments spend more on services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark income; 1 mark demand for services [2]

items.stem: In Country P, 35% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 31% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. What percentage work in the tertiary sector?
Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the increasing links and interdependence between countries through trade, investment, communication and culture”.
items.answer: Globalisation
items.markingKey: Globalisation: the increasing links and interdependence between countries through trade, investment, communication and culture. [1]

items.stem: Explain the advantages TNCs can bring to host countries.
items.answer: Jobs and regular wages; training and skills; investment in infrastructure; taxes; export earnings; a multiplier effect on local suppliers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the disadvantages TNCs can bring to host countries.
items.answer: Low wages and poor working conditions; profits leave the country; environmental pollution; local firms cannot compete; jobs can be lost if the TNC relocates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Name one example of a transnational corporation (TNC) you have studied and, for that example, evaluate the impacts of the TNC on the host country.
items.answer: Samsung in Vietnam: Benefits: jobs, skills, infrastructure and a multiplier effect on local suppliers; export earnings. Problems: long hours, heavy reliance on one company, most profits and high-value parts remain in South Korea, environmental concerns.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Economic, social and environmental advantages and disadvantages with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: For Samsung in Vietnam or another example of a transnational corporation (TNC), briefly describe how the TNC operates in different countries.
items.answer: Samsung in Vietnam: South Korean TNC; huge smartphone factories at Bac Ninh and Thai Nguyen in northern Vietnam since 2008, employing over 100 000 workers; Samsung accounts for about a fifth of Vietnam’s exports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Headquarters, research, manufacturing locations, workforce, global supply chain. [4]

items.stem: Name one example of a transnational corporation (TNC) you have studied and, for that example, describe how the TNC operates in different countries.
items.answer: Nike: Headquarters in Oregon, USA, where design, research and marketing take place; shoes and clothing made by about 500 contract factories in about 35 countries employing about 1 million workers, mainly in Vietnam, China and Indonesia.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Headquarters, research, manufacturing locations, workforce, global supply chain. [4]

items.stem: For a named example of a transnational corporation (TNC) that you have studied, evaluate the impacts of the TNC on the host country.
items.answer: Model answer (Toyota in the UK): Benefits: skilled jobs, investment in a region that lost traditional industry, multiplier effect, exports. Problems: profits return to Japan; the plant depends on trade rules (Brexit created uncertainty); greenfield site lost farmland.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Economic, social and environmental advantages and disadvantages with a judgement. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Name an example of a transnational corporation (TNC). For your chosen example, evaluate the impacts of the TNC on the host country.
items.answer: Model answer (Samsung in Vietnam): Benefits: jobs, skills, infrastructure and a multiplier effect on local suppliers; export earnings. Problems: long hours, heavy reliance on one company, most profits and high-value parts remain in South Korea, environmental concerns.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Economic, social and environmental advantages and disadvantages with a judgement. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: A student writes: “TNCs only bring benefits to LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They create jobs but can pay low wages, cause pollution and send profits abroad.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 shows how the US$100 price of a pair of trainers made in Vietnam is shared: retailer 45%, brand (TNC) profit and marketing 20%, materials 12%, transport and taxes 10%, factory workers’ wages 13%. Suggest why so little of the price goes to the workers.
items.answer: Labour is cheap and plentiful in Vietnam; workers have little bargaining power; most value is added by design, branding and retailing in HICs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 shows how the US$100 price of a pair of trainers made in Vietnam is shared: retailer 35%, brand (TNC) profit and marketing 30%, materials 10%, transport and taxes 8%, factory workers’ wages 17%. (a) Calculate how many times more the retailer receives than the factory workers. (b) Suggest a suitable way of presenting these data.
items.answer: (a) 2.1 times (b) A pie chart or divided bar, because the data are parts of a whole adding to 100%.
items.markingKey: (a) 35 ÷ 17 [1] (b) 1 mark technique; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Name an example of a transnational corporation (TNC). For your chosen example, describe how the TNC operates in different countries.
items.answer: Model answer (Samsung in Vietnam): South Korean TNC; huge smartphone factories at Bac Ninh and Thai Nguyen in northern Vietnam since 2008, employing over 100 000 workers; Samsung accounts for about a fifth of Vietnam’s exports.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Headquarters, research, manufacturing locations, workforce, global supply chain. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a composite measure of development from 0 to 1 combining life expectancy, years of schooling and GNI per capita”.
items.answer: Human Development Index (HDI)
items.markingKey: Human Development Index (HDI): a composite measure of development from 0 to 1 combining life expectancy, years of schooling and GNI per capita. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “A country with a high GNI per capita always has a high quality of life for everyone.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. GNI is an average; wealth may be very unevenly distributed and social measures may be poor.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why a composite indicator such as the HDI gives a better picture of development.
items.answer: It combines economic (income) and social (health, education) measures, so a country that is rich but has poor health or education is not ranked too highly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark combines; 1 mark example/reason [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows development indicators for selected countries. Niger: GNI per capita US$600, life expectancy 62 years, HDI 0.39. Norway: GNI per capita US$95 000, life expectancy 83 years, HDI 0.97. Bangladesh: GNI per capita US$2 700, life expectancy 73 years, HDI 0.67. Brazil: GNI per capita US$9 000, life expectancy 76 years, HDI 0.76. Suggest why a country may have a high GNI per capita but a lower life expectancy than expected.
items.answer: Wealth is unequally distributed, little spent on health care, poor diet or lifestyle diseases, conflict or high HIV rates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: A student tests the hypothesis “Countries with higher GNI per capita have higher life expectancy.” using six countries: Japan: US$42 000, 84 years. China: US$13 000, 78 years. Brazil: US$9 000, 76 years. Bangladesh: US$2 700, 73 years. India: US$2 400, 70 years. UK: US$49 000, 81 years. (a) State what the result shows about the hypothesis. (b) Explain why a sample of six countries limits the conclusion.
items.answer: (a) A strong positive correlation, so the hypothesis is supported. (b) A small sample may not be representative and the result could be due to chance; more countries from each income group are needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark interpretation linked to value [1] (b) 1 mark small/unrepresentative; 1 mark improvement [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows development indicators for selected countries. Japan: GNI per capita US$42 000, life expectancy 84 years, HDI 0.92. Niger: GNI per capita US$600, life expectancy 62 years, HDI 0.39. Norway: GNI per capita US$95 000, life expectancy 83 years, HDI 0.97. Brazil: GNI per capita US$9 000, life expectancy 76 years, HDI 0.76. China: GNI per capita US$13 000, life expectancy 78 years, HDI 0.79. (a) Calculate how many times greater the highest GNI per capita is than the lowest. (b) Rank the countries by HDI from highest to lowest. (c) Suggest one other indicator that could be added to the table, and explain why.

items.markingKey: (a) 95 000 ÷ 600 = 158.3 [2] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark indicator; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a poorer, often remote area of a country with less investment and lower incomes”.
items.answer: Periphery
items.markingKey: Periphery: a poorer, often remote area of a country with less investment and lower incomes. [1]

items.stem: Explain how fair trade helps to reduce inequality.
items.answer: Farmers receive a guaranteed minimum price and a premium for community projects such as schools and clean water; better working conditions and stable incomes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark price; 1 mark premium/community [2]

items.stem: Table 3.2 shows mean income per person (US$) and adult literacy (%) by region in a large MIC. North: $5 000, 90%. North-east: $3 000, 81%. Centre: $7 000, 89%. South-east: $18 000, 98%. South: $14 000, 96%. (a) Calculate the difference in income between the richest and poorest regions. (b) Calculate how many times greater income is in the richest region than the poorest.
“Aid is the most effective way to reduce the development gap.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Emergency and long-term aid can fund health, education and infrastructure; debt relief frees money for services. Against: Fair trade, investment by TNCs, good governance and microfinance can be more sustainable; aid may be misused or create dependency. Judgement: Aid helps most when targeted and combined with fair trade and investment; on its own it is rarely enough.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “primary sector”?
options: Jobs that provide services, such as teaching, health care, retail and transport.
Jobs that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining.
Jobs that process raw materials or make manufactured goods, such as car assembly.
Jobs in research, information and high technology, such as software development and scientific research.
items.answer: Jobs that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining.
items.markingKey: Primary sector: jobs that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining. [1]

items.stem: Explain the effects of deindustrialisation on a region.
items.answer: Unemployment, loss of skills, derelict factories and land, out-migration of young people, decline of local shops and services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: In Country Q, 71% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 9% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. Describe how these data would be plotted on a triangular graph.
items.answer: Each side is a 0-100% scale for one sector; read primary, secondary and tertiary along their gridlines; the point where the three lines meet is plotted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark three axes; 1 mark plotting point [2]

items.stem: In Country Q, 24% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 33% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. (a) Calculate the percentage employed in the tertiary sector. (b) The workforce is 20 million. Calculate how many people work in the primary sector. (c) Is this country most likely to be an LIC, an NEE or an HIC? Give a reason.
items.answer: (a) 43% (b) 4.8 million (c) NEE: a large secondary sector (33%) as industry grows, with primary falling (24%).
items.markingKey: (a) 100 − 24 − 33 = 43% [1] (b) 20 × 24% = 4.8 million [1] (c) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark use of data [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Globalisation has increased trade between countries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Lower tariffs, cheap shipping and the internet have increased world trade greatly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why globalisation has increased.
items.answer: Container shipping and air freight; the internet and telecommunications; trade agreements reducing tariffs; growth of TNCs and FDI; global finance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Study your case study of a transnational corporation (TNC) (for example Samsung in Vietnam). Briefly describe how the TNC operates in different countries.
items.answer: Samsung in Vietnam: South Korean TNC; huge smartphone factories at Bac Ninh and Thai Nguyen in northern Vietnam since 2008, employing over 100 000 workers; Samsung accounts for about a fifth of Vietnam’s exports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Headquarters, research, manufacturing locations, workforce, global supply chain. [4]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 shows how the US$150 price of a pair of trainers made in Vietnam is shared: retailer 45%, brand (TNC) profit and marketing 20%, materials 15%, transport and taxes 8%, factory workers’ wages 12%. (a) Calculate the amount paid to factory workers. (b) Calculate how many times more the retailer receives than the factory workers.
items.answer: (a) US$18 (b) 3.8 times

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 shows how the US$150 price of a pair of trainers made in Vietnam is shared: retailer 45%, brand (TNC) profit and marketing 25%, materials 12%, transport and taxes 8%, factory workers’ wages 10%. (a) Calculate the amount paid to factory workers. (b) Suggest a suitable way of presenting these data.
items.answer: (a) US$15 (b) A pie chart or divided bar, because the data are parts of a whole adding to 100%.
items.markingKey: (a) 10% × 150 [1] (b) 1 mark technique; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Omar argues that the benefits of TNCs for host countries outweigh the problems. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: jobs and wages; environment.
items.answer: For: TNCs bring jobs, wages, skills, infrastructure and export earnings (e.g. Samsung in Vietnam); the multiplier effect helps local firms. Against: Low wages and poor conditions (Rana Plaza 2013); profit leakage; pollution; dependence on footloose investment. Judgement: For many NEEs the benefits have outweighed the problems, provided governments regulate working conditions and the environment.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an adjustment to income figures that takes account of differences in the cost of living between countries”.
items.answer: Purchasing power parity (PPP)
items.markingKey: Purchasing power parity (PPP): an adjustment to income figures that takes account of differences in the cost of living between countries. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “The HDI has a maximum value of 1.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It runs from 0 to 1; Norway and Switzerland score about 0.96-0.97.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “Infant mortality is usually higher in LICs than in HICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “A country with a high GNI per capita always has a high quality of life for everyone.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Poor health care, nutrition and sanitation cause more infant deaths. (b) Not correct. GNI is an average; wealth may be very unevenly distributed and social measures may be poor.

items.stem: A student tests the hypothesis “Countries with higher GNI per capita have higher life expectancy.” using six countries: Niger: US$600, 62 years. Brazil: US$9 000, 76 years. Bangladesh: US$2 700, 73 years. China: US$13 000, 78 years. Mexico: US$11 000, 75 years. India: US$2 400, 70 years. Rank the countries for GNI per capita and for life expectancy (1 = highest).
items.answer: Niger 6/6; Brazil 3/2; Bangladesh 4/4; China 1/1; Mexico 2/3; India 5/5
items.markingKey: 1 mark each correct set of ranks (tied values share the mean rank) [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows development indicators for selected countries. Norway: GNI per capita US$95 000, life expectancy 83 years, HDI 0.97. Japan: GNI per capita US$42 000, life expectancy 84 years, HDI 0.92. Brazil: GNI per capita US$9 000, life expectancy 76 years, HDI 0.76. India: GNI per capita US$2 400, life expectancy 70 years, HDI 0.64. Nigeria: GNI per capita US$2 100, life expectancy 54 years, HDI 0.55. (a) Describe the relationship between GNI per capita and life expectancy shown in Table 3.1. (b) Rank the countries by HDI from highest to lowest.
items.answer: (a) Positive: countries with higher GNI per capita generally have higher life expectancy, though Norway is an exception. (b) Norway, Japan, Brazil, India, Nigeria
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark relationship; 1 mark data/exception [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: A student tests the hypothesis “Countries with higher GNI per capita have higher life expectancy.” using six countries: Japan: US$42 000, 84 years. Brazil: US$9 000, 76 years. Niger: US$600, 62 years. Nigeria: US$2 100, 54 years. Kenya: US$2 100, 63 years. China: US$13 000, 78 years. (a) Rank the countries for GNI per capita and for life expectancy (1 = highest). (b) Calculate Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient using rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n³ − n).
items.answer: (a) Japan 1/1; Brazil 3/3; Niger 6/5; Nigeria 4.5/6; Kenya 4.5/4; China 2/2 (b) rs = 0.9
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each correct set of ranks (tied values share the mean rank) [2] (b) Σd² = 3.5; 1 − 6 × 3.5 ÷ (6³ − 6) = 0.9 [3]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “differences in wealth and quality of life between regions of the same country”.
items.answer: Regional inequality
items.markingKey: Regional inequality: differences in wealth and quality of life between regions of the same country. [1]

items.stem: Explain why debt can slow development.
items.answer: Money spent repaying loans and interest cannot be spent on health, education and infrastructure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark repayment; 1 mark opportunity cost [2]

items.stem: Table 3.2 shows mean income per person (US$) and adult literacy (%) by region in an emerging economy. North: $3 000, 87%. North-east: $3 000, 80%. Centre: $10 000, 89%. South-east: $18 000, 98%. South: $11 000, 93%. (a) Calculate the difference in income between the richest and poorest regions. (b) Calculate how many times greater income is in the richest region than the poorest.
For a named example of regional inequality within a country that you have studied, explain why there are differences in development between regions.
items.answer: Model answer (India): Investment in ports and IT in western and southern states; better education and health spending in Kerala; high population density and reliance on farming in Bihar; poor infrastructure in rural states.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Physical, historical, economic and social causes, cumulative causation. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “secondary sector”?
options: Jobs that provide services, such as teaching, health care, retail and transport.
The percentage of the workforce employed in each sector of the economy.
Jobs in research, information and high technology, such as software development and scientific research.
Jobs that process raw materials or make manufactured goods, such as car assembly.
items.answer: Jobs that process raw materials or make manufactured goods, such as car assembly.
items.markingKey: Secondary sector: jobs that process raw materials or make manufactured goods, such as car assembly. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “All tertiary jobs are low-paid.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The tertiary sector includes highly paid jobs such as doctors and lawyers as well as low-paid ones.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: In Country R, 33% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 32% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. Explain how the employment structure may change in the next 30 years.
items.answer: Secondary may peak then fall as wages rise and automation increases; tertiary and quaternary will grow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark change; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: In Country R, 3% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 17% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. (a) Is this country most likely to be an LIC, an NEE or an HIC? Give a reason. (b) Describe how these data would be plotted on a triangular graph.
items.answer: (a) HIC: very few in primary (3%) and most in services (80%). (b) Each side is a 0-100% scale for one sector; read primary, secondary and tertiary along their gridlines; the point where the three lines meet is plotted.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark use of data [2] (b) 1 mark three axes; 1 mark plotting point [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “A TNC may close a factory if costs rise.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. TNCs are “footloose” and may move production to cheaper locations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “A TNC may close a factory if costs rise.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the disadvantages TNCs can bring to host countries.
items.answer: (a) Correct. TNCs are “footloose” and may move production to cheaper locations. (b) Low wages and poor working conditions; profits leave the country; environmental pollution; local firms cannot compete; jobs can be lost if the TNC relocates.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: For Toyota in the UK or another example of a transnational corporation (TNC), briefly describe how the TNC operates in different countries.
items.answer: Toyota in the UK: Japanese TNC with a car factory at Burnaston near Derby (opened 1992) and an engine plant in Deeside, Wales; employs about 2500-3000 people directly and supports many local suppliers; cars exported mainly to Europe.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Headquarters, research, manufacturing locations, workforce, global supply chain. [4]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 shows how the US$120 price of a pair of trainers made in Vietnam is shared: retailer 40%, brand (TNC) profit and marketing 30%, materials 15%, transport and taxes 10%, factory workers’ wages 5%. Suggest a suitable way of presenting these data.
items.answer: A pie chart or divided bar, because the data are parts of a whole adding to 100%.
items.markingKey: 1 mark technique; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 shows how the US$100 price of a pair of trainers made in Vietnam is shared: retailer 35%, brand (TNC) profit and marketing 30%, materials 15%, transport and taxes 10%, factory workers’ wages 10%. (a) Calculate the amount paid to factory workers. (b) Suggest a suitable way of presenting these data.
items.answer: (a) US$10 (b) A pie chart or divided bar, because the data are parts of a whole adding to 100%.
items.markingKey: (a) 10% × 100 [1] (b) 1 mark technique; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 shows how the US$150 price of a pair of trainers made in Vietnam is shared: retailer 45%, brand (TNC) profit and marketing 20%, materials 10%, transport and taxes 8%, factory workers’ wages 17%. (a) Calculate the amount paid to factory workers. (b) Suggest why so little of the price goes to the workers. (c) Explain one benefit and one problem for Vietnam of making trainers for a TNC.
items.answer: (a) US$25.5 (b) Labour is cheap and plentiful in Vietnam; workers have little bargaining power; most value is added by design, branding and retailing in HICs. (c) Benefit: jobs and regular wages, export earnings, skills. Problem: low wages and long hours, profits go abroad, factories could move to cheaper countries.
items.markingKey: (a) 17% × 150 [1] (b) 1 mark each up to [2] (c) 1 mark each with development [4]
